brief.topic: Why the Middle Measurement Counts Four Times

s01: Three height measurements can determine the area under a parabola.
Take x squared from zero to two. Its heights are zero, one, and four.
A straight line between the endpoints gives a trapezoid of area four.
A rectangle using only the middle height gives area two.
For a quadratic, combine two thirds of the midpoint estimate with one third of the trapezoid estimate.
That gives eight thirds. It is the exact area here.
In terms of the heights, the weights become one, four, one, multiplied by the interval width divided by six.
The middle receives four times each endpoint weight. This is Simpson's rule.
Why can that work? A quadratic is a sum of a constant, a linear term, and a squared term.
These weights integrate each of those three pieces exactly. Adding the pieces preserves exactness.
Try x to the fourth power on the same interval.
The three heights now give twenty thirds, while the exact integral is thirty two fifths.
The values differ. For general curves this is an approximation, improved by using more subintervals with suitable smoothness.

scenes.narration:
Three height measurements can determine the area under a parabola. Take x squared from zero to two. Its heights are zero, one, and four.

A straight line between the endpoints gives a trapezoid of area four. A rectangle using only the middle height gives area two. For a quadratic, combine two thirds of the midpoint estimate with one third of the trapezoid estimate.

That gives eight thirds. It is the exact area here. In terms of the heights, the weights become one, four, one, multiplied by the interval width divided by six. The middle receives four times each endpoint weight. This is Simpson's rule.

Why can that work? A quadratic is a sum of a constant, a linear term, and a squared term. These weights integrate each of those three pieces exactly. Adding the pieces preserves exactness.

Try x to the fourth power on the same interval. The three heights now give twenty thirds, while the exact integral is thirty two fifths. The values differ. For general curves this is an approximation, improved by using more subintervals with suitable smoothness.
